To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) courts have responded inconsistently and unsatisfyingly to the Borat Problem; (2) the Borat Problem is best understood as a problem of bilateral opportunistic behavior; (3) the problem can be solved by requiring specific assent to standard form terms and requiring non-drafting parties to satisfy a heightened burden of proof before challenging the enforceability of such terms; and (4) the proposed solutions are consistent with established contract and tort law doctrine.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the Borat problem should be solved by requiring that a party who drafts a standard form contract must obtain the specific assent of its counterpart to any terms that contradict prior oral representations, and that a party who is not a draftsman must satisfy a heightened evidential standard before being permitted on a motion for summary judgment or at trial to prove fraud or misrepresentation in order to avoid the application of standard form terms.

The main takeaway from our work is that
courts should not hesitate to impose a specific assent requirement when the terms of a standard form contract contradict or disclaim a prior representation.
the law of contracts should focus on ensuring that the parties to standard form contracts are aware of what they are signing and that they understand the terms of those contracts.
courts should be more careful in distinguishing between fraud, which is a tort, and the misrepresentation or non-performance of a promise, which is a breach of contract.
